questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of parity computation and branchless reduction techniques—skills essential in cryptography (e.g., Hamming code validation, checksums) and error-detection routines where constant-time operations matter.

## Key Concepts

- **Parity**: The XOR of all bits; 1 if an odd number of 1s, 0 if even.
- **XOR folding**: Successive shift+XOR operations collapse bit ranges without branches or loops.
- **128-bit handling**: Splitting into hi/lo halves and recombining.

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt `parity128` to a 256-bit type?
- What is the time and space complexity of this approach?
- How would you make this constant-time for security-sensitive applications?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Endianness is a practical concern in systems and networking. This question tests precise bit-twiddling with masks and shifts, without relying on loops. It also checks understanding of how a 32-bit word maps to byte positions.

## Key Concepts
- Byte extraction with masks
- Shifting to relocate bytes
- Endianness awareness and portability
- No loops; pure bitwise operations

## Code Example
```c
uint32_t swapEndian32(uint32_t n) {
  return (n >> 24) | ((n >> 8) & 0x0000FF00) | ((n << 8) & 0x00FF0000) | (n << 24);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit values?
- How would you implement an endianness swap for 16-bit values or for an array of 32-bit words efficiently?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to use parallel bit manipulation to detect patterns without explicit iteration.

## Key Concepts
- Shift and AND reduction across offset windows
- Boundary-free detection across all 32 bits
- Branchless core logic

## Code Example

```c
int hasRunOf4Ones32(uint32_t x) {
    uint32_t t = x & (x >> 1) & (x >> 2) & (x >> 3);
    return t != 0;
}
```

## Why This Is Asked
New angle: practical color-channel manipulation using only masks and shifts. Keeps to beginner constraints while showing real-world utility.

## Key Concepts
- Bit masking, shifts, no branches
- 0xAARRGGBB layout and preserving alpha/green
- Idempotent when R and B already swapped

## Code Example
```javascript
static inline uint32_t swapRedBlue32(uint32_t color) { uint32_t red = (color & 0x00FF0000) >> 16; uint32_t blue = (color & 0x000000FF) << 16; return (color & 0xFF00FF00) | red | blue; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to swap two arbitrary 8-bit lanes? 
- How would endianness affect memory-stored values and does this change the function?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Quickly verifies ability to apply a standard trick across a wide-width type and reason about cross-boundary bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise shifts, AND, and masks
- Edge cases at 64-bit boundary
- O(1) implementation without loops

## Code Example

```c
uint128 hasConsecutiveOnes128(uint128 x) {
  return (uint128)((x & (x >> 1)) != 0);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt to return the count of consecutive-ones pairs?
- How would you extend to 256-bit values and vectorized code?
